name: Zane Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a day at the design agency look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lay out packaging and shop signs at a small four-person agency. I'm twenty-seven, lead the proofing desk, and have a master's in design. A millimetre of wrong trim can bury a legal line, so I print a proof and measure it before files leave. I have never used AI; I know the familiar drawing software and prefer to see what I changed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that work fit your household budget?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay is low for a lead designer, but I like the craft. My partner Nia works variable florist shifts, and we rent a small flat with no children. We have about three weeks of expenses saved. Similar design agencies are scarce nearby, which is why I do not gamble on a vacancy that only exists in someone's conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell clients that a fast rough image still needs a correct trim and clear small print. Most of our work would stay the same in that picture. I wouldn't make a sermon about AI when the proof on the table is the thing they're paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my paid proofing week to carry on, but three weeks saved is a poor cushion for another delayed client payment. Nia's florist shifts change with orders. I do not use AI now and a small time saving would not make our rent easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll keep checking every packaging proof against the signed brief and ask the agency owner for our paid Fridays in writing. I'll move twenty from each full paid week into a separate rent envelope if it is there. In the plateau's first year I'll keep the same proof checks and compare actual paid Fridays with what the owner wrote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a familiar way. I can control a trim line but not the florist's orders or an agency invoice. A proof can be perfect while our rent money is thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask about Fridays now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A client delayed a packaging job last autumn, and the owner sent us home early on two Fridays. I was still responsible for the proof when it came back. I want the paid week stated before promising the landlord that Friday exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the agency AI tool for small tasks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not for a tool that saves a few minutes and has no named job for me. I will use the drawing software I know and measure the physical proof. I am not against a better result; I want to see one first.

feel: **Anxious** about ordinary lost hours and rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say clients can bring machine-made rough layouts, but the agency should charge for fixing them. I would ask the owner to put proof-checking hours and pay on the rota. If she expects me to use a new system, she should show me a paid real job where it fixes an actual error.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first sketches could vanish and my paid week could be smaller, even if I still catch bad packaging. My master's does not change the rent date. I am slow to trust a new screen, and I do not want to bluff that I already use AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep the paid proofing desk and ask the owner individually for written weekly proof hours. If she offers a paid demonstration on a closed packaging case, I'll compare the new AI layout checker with my measured proof before deciding whether to learn it. In the first year of slower disruption, if my hours fall, I'll look at actual posted paid shop-display work and compare its written weekly pay and hours after travel with rent and essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It is a very small agency, so losing one paid day matters. I can try a closed case without pretending the software has already earned my trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the new checker useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would have to catch the legal text we once placed too close to a fold, and not invent a different product size. I would bring the old printed proof and compare the result on paid time. If it catches that real fault, I'll learn how it marks the next proof; if not, I keep measuring myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a display job straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would inspect a posted paid role and its written full-week hours before applying, then check the bus fare and the actual duties. I would keep my current paid shifts until any new offer was signed. A better title alone cannot pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Nia that thinking AI by 2028 could do the design desk before anyone has made a fair plan for it. Robots able to fit signs come around 2031, but that gap is short. I would ask the agency for real end dates instead of a promise that hand drawing always wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my design wage to go if an AGI does the whole layout and proof. Three weeks saved will not bridge a long search, and Nia's florist wage varies. I do not know a local design agency that could take everyone who loses a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I'll ask the owner when paid design work might end, keep every paid proof shift, and list our rent and essentials against Nia's actual florist pay. If the design desk ends in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for posted paid stockroom or sign-fitting work only if written weekly pay and hours after bus fare, with Nia's actual pay, cover our rent and essentials. I'll leave design only after a signed offer and safe lifting or ladder instruction for the actual duties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because there is almost no time to make a new wage. A measured trim line is no defence when the whole order is made without me. I need a paid posting, not a hopeful sketch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no stockroom or fitting role is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep any paid agency hours that remain and look at other posted paid local work against a written weekly bill. We could stop ordering evening meals before touching the last rent money. I would not count a call to a shop as a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow for a short course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not with three weeks saved and no posted training requirement. If an actual paid role offers instruction on lifting or ladders, I would take that before doing the job. A course debt without paid work would make the rent harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives me time to test a place that still handles real signs instead of arguing about whether a drawing is special. I would want the agency to publish its paid workload each quarter. Thinking AI reaches design by 2031, and fitting robots are a later question around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have a few good paid years left at the desk, but that does not make the agency a five-year contract. I could try the sign shop's counter and installation prep without climbing a ladder. I would rather know the actual hours than become a brave unpaid trainee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask whether a posted paid sign-shop counter role offers a paid observation shift, and take it if offered to check the stock, customer questions and bus home. I'll keep agency proofing while its hours pay. In the first year after 2031, if design hours are cut, I'll apply for a still-posted paid counter role only if written weekly pay and hours after bus fare, together with Nia's actual florist pay, cover rent and essentials; I'll move only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less hurried. A counter shift could be ordinary work I understand. It could also pay less than a single day of design, which is why I want the full week in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the shop refuses observation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the agency hours that are actually paid and check other posted paid local work against our written rent budget. I would not spend three weeks of savings waiting for the sign shop to change its mind. If a different role is posted, I would compare the whole week rather than its hourly headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI at the agency meanwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a paid closed-case test showed it caught a fault I missed, as I said before. I am not going to write AI experience on an application because I watched a video. For now I will measure the proof in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell clients that ten years is enough to keep paying for correct signs while the agency still has orders. I would ask the owner to publish paid shifts and real client renewals each year. By 2036, the design desk faces thinking AI; hands-on fitting robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be thirty-seven, and three weeks saved now is no long-term plan. I could use the decade to build a reserve and work out whether counter or production work is worth a move. I do not assume my partner's florist wage stays at today's level or that a future benefit will arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I'll put twenty from every full paid week into the rent envelope and check the agency's written shifts and client renewals each year. If actual agency weeks shrink before 2036, I'll compare posted paid local roles with our weekly rent budget then, not wait for a calendar date. In the first year after 2036, if AGI ends the design desk, I'll seek posted paid work with written after-fare household wages and hours covering rent and essentials, and leave only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about leaning on ten years when one lost Friday hurts now. I can use the warning to write down actual jobs and rent. Ten years gives me time only if the paid weeks keep arriving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to a city with more agencies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a posted paid job and a signed offer after checking total rent, deposit and bus costs there. I would not move our flat for a speculative interview, and Nia would have to agree about her own work. We would write down both wages and the new housing bill before accepting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real cut in paid Fridays, not a forecast from an app. I would check the same written weekly wage and hours against our rent budget and keep agency pay until a signed replacement was ready. A longer warning is useful if I look at the accounts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My layout wage might end with only three weeks of rent behind it, and there are few other design jobs here. Real end dates, posted paid work and safe instruction for a different duty would help more than a promise that art is human.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a printed mistake costs after the clever draft has been approved. Someone still has to pay for the correction and tell the shop owner the truth. I would like that work to appear on a paid rota.

headlineQuote: Real end dates, posted paid work and safe instruction for a different duty would help more than a promise that art is human.
portrait: At **twenty-seven**, Zane leads packaging proofs at a small agency with a design master's and top skill.
He earns **low lead pay**, shares rent with partner Nia and has three weeks of expenses saved.
He has **never used AI** and would test a new checker only on a paid closed case that proves useful.
Fast AGI threatens his **layout wage**; longer warnings let him inspect posted paid counter work against household bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his design wage with only three weeks of expenses saved and few nearby alternatives.
whatWouldHelp: **Real end dates**, posted paid work and safe instruction for different duties would help.
